delta_name: Timing closure dominated by wire delay → cell + variation delay
at_28nm: Long wires dominated path delay; buffer insertion, useful-skew, and gate sizing on long nets were the leverage points. Interconnect RC mattered more than transistor variation.
at_7nm_5nm: Cell intrinsic delay and random device variation (per-fin Vt spread, LG/LER) dominate. Hold/margin budgets are set by σ-of-delay tails, not by wirelength. Useful-skew is mostly a recovery lever, not a primary one.
why_it_changed: Resistance per unit length of BEOL scales sub-linearly with node, but logic-stage delay and transistor stochastic variation scale up with fin pitch, fin count variability, and thinner FOx. Path delay is sliced into more shorter stages, each carrying its own σ.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer chases wirelength and adds more buffers/sizing on long nets, expecting ~80% of slacks there. Atnm the path is already buffer-saturated by the synthesis/place solution; residual slack is in σ, not in C*load. Symptom: tools report 'no setup' after exhaustive buffer sweeps, but Monte-Carlo or AOCV-style derates show paths with negative σ-margin that never appear in nominal STA.
workflow_impact: Variation-aware timing (AOCV/SOCV/LVF) and statistical derate generation move upstream into placement and into signoff margin budgeting. Slack histograms (not single-corner WNS) become the closure metric.

at_28nm: Congestion meant 'not enough routing tracks per gcell.' Fixes: spread cells, raise utilization slowly, change block aspect, partial blockage. Pin access was rarely the gating problem.
at_7nm_5nm: Congestion is pin-access-driven: each cell has many fewer routing tracks per pin, higher pin density per cell, and the routing solution is limited by how many unique colors/vias can land on a pin shape, not by horizontal track supply.
why_it_changed: Tighter contacted poly pitch (CPP) and minimum metal pitch shrink the per-pin track count faster than the cell library's pin pattern is redesigned; multi-patterning needs more unidirectional tracks and color-equalization that further reduce legal pin landing options.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer treats congestion as a placement-density / utilization problem and tightens the placement to 'use the routing resources better.' Symptom: pin-short and pin-access DRC errors explode in route, often invisible until detailed route, even though global route shows little overflow.
workflow_impact: Pin-access analysis and pin-shape/legal-pin-shape checking become a placement-time constraint, and placer cost functions explicitly carry pin-access shortage. Cell swapping to multi-pin variants and pin-layer-aware placement are first-class passes, not post-route cleanups.

delta_name: DRC dominated by width/space → via/pin-access + multi-patterning DRC
at_28nm: DRC was mostly width/space, enclosure, end-of-line. A handful of rules; fixable by ECO routing and minor layer swaps.
at_7nm_5nm: Rule sets are dominated by multi-patterning (same-color spacing, color-balanced fill, double-via everywhere), cut-layer spacing, via-pillar/enclosure, and BEOL-end metal/fin-shaping checks. Number of rules and rule-checks rises by an order of magnitude.
why_it_changed: 193i immersion multi-patterning and SADP/SAQP fin patterning cannot reliably resolve arbitrary polygons; pitch and coloring must be enforced as geometry constraints, not just lithography-checked later. EOP and EUV relaxes some LELE rules but SADP-finned BEOL still needs color constraints in the stack.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer defers DRC cleanup to a post-route 'fixing' ECO and expects a clean chip within a few thousand short violations. Symptom: hundred-thousands of color/decoloration/equivalent-via violations that interact with each other and with timing; clean-up is no longer incremental.
workflow_impact: Coloring, via-doubling, and pattern-aware DRC are moved into global/detailed route engines and into placement (legalization against color maps). DRC signoff shifts from 'check, then fix' to 'prevent during route.'

delta_name: Power/ground a background resource → P/G vs routing-resource tension
at_28nm: Power straps were a back-end finishing step; Mx stripe pitch was driven mostly by EM/IR budgets, not by competing for tracks with signal.
at_7nm_5nm: Power-stripe pitch competes with signal tracks on every routing layer because the BEOL stack has fewer dedicated 'power-only' layers and thicker power bars consume routing capacity. IR-drop target and EM target fight each other and fight signal-routing.
why_it_changed: BEOL stack thickness scaling and resistance per unit length not improving as fast as resistance-per-via; you need more, wider, denser straps closer to the standard cells to hold IR within a few percent of Vdd, but those same upper layers are now useful signal-routing resources.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer sets P/G pitch by 'typical' EM and lets signal routing use upper metals freely. Symptom: dynamic IR-drop hotspots late in the schedule once route is frozen, requiring wholesale P/G restructure that destroys route and timing.
workflow_impact: Early P/G planning (often called powerplanning) becomes a stage that informs placement and blockage, not a back-end finishing task. Power-aware placement and IR-aware optimization are first-class timing/closure drivers.

Placement mostly uniform-density → multi-patterning/coloring aware placement
at_28nm: Placement optimized for timing, area-congestion; poly/fin patterning was effectively transparent to the placer.
at_7nm_5nm: Placement must respect poly/fin color, gate-color balance (for fin splitting, dummy-fin, fin depopulation), cut-layer coloring, and via pillar placement. Cells can be on disallowed colors; placement legalization remaps.
why_it_changed: Fin/sheet patterning at 7nm and beyond is done with SADP/SAQP; fin direction and dummy-fin density are constrained by lithography and stress. Uniform poly density and fin continuity over a minimum length are required to avoid patterning failures and variability.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer hands the placer a single density map and expects uniform white space. Symptom: post-route pattern-density and fin-density DRC fail locally even with legal placement; recovery requires cell swaps, color-aware placement, and on some nodes explicit fin-decoration/fill synthesis.
workflow_impact: Placer inputs include color maps, fincor/metal-decor layers, and disallowed-site maps. Legalizer does color remapping; placement feedback loops with the pattern/decor synthesis stage.

delta_name: Library/multi-Vt strategy: 2–3 Vts, simple swap → fine Vt/fin-count granularity, swap-driven closure
at_28nm: Typical library: HVT, SVT, LVT (sometimes ULVT). Swapping to LVT was a small, localized ECO step after timing was mostly closed.
at_7nm_5nm: Library explosion: many Vt steps, multiple channel/fin options per cell, and Vt/fin swaps are an iterative closure lever used throughout timing closure, not just an ECO. Threshold-voltage granularity is finer than the cell swap slack resolution.
why_it_changed: Vt spread per unit area is reduced to control leakage, and leakage is a much larger fraction of total power at 7nm/5nm Vdd. Designers need finer control of leakage vs delay trade-off per region, and dynamic power is low enough that a small per-cell leakage increase is acceptable.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer defers Vt/fin swaps to 'when we run out of slack.' Symptom: route and timing converge but block-level leakage is multiples above target; swapping many cells to fix leakage breaks timing; thermal/IR analysis fails late.
workflow_impact: Vt/fin swapping is interleaved with placement, optimization, and clock-tree stages. Power-aware timing is run continuously, not as a final check.

delta_name: Clock distribution: balanced H-tree + mesh-light → mesh-heavy + useful-skew + deskew loops
at_28nm: Clock was largely a balanced H-tree/spine with a coarse mesh; useful skew was a small, manual lever. Skew target dominated by process, not OCV derate.
at_7nm_5nm: Clock is a dense mesh with structured spines/leaves, large intentional useful skew, and OCV derate dominates skew budget. CTS is iterative with optimization and re-runs many times; clock becomes the largest single net and is built after coarse placement.
why_it_changed: Per-device OCV and PVT variation scale with node; nominal skew is small compared to derate-adjusted skew, so the only way to recover timing is to use intentional skew and a robust low-skew distribution that is less sensitive to on-chip variation.
what_breaks: A 28nm-trained engineer builds a 'skew-minimal' tree first and applies small useful skew to critical paths. Symptom: hold fails massively across the chip because OCV derate exceeds intentional skew; large-scale mesh restructuring late.
workflow_impact: Clock planning starts early and is part of placement blockage / regional synthesis. CTS and useful-skew optimization are interleaved with placement and legalization; signoff runs AOCV/SOCV + reconvergence pessimism removal as part of closure.

Signoff corners: 4–6 PVT corners → corne: Signoff ran a handful of corners: typically SS/FF/SF/FS at hot/cold with two Vdd; flat derates.
at_7nm_5nm: Corner count explodes (SS/FF, hot/cold, multiple Vdd for DVFS, aging corners, mixed-Vt corners, plus AOCV/SOCV/LVF) and is combined with statistical derate lookup tables per cell/path-depth/stage.
why_it_changed: Variability increases fin count, channel length, and voltage; bias-temperature instability and HCI aging must be modeled as their own corners. Multi-railulti-Vt designs and DVFS multiply the corner space.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer scopes signoff to 'worst-case setup' and 'worst-case hold' corners. Symptom: paths pass in nominal and worst corners fail in mixed or aging corners; signoff reports vary wildly depending on which subset of corners is run, and tape risk shifts to late-found aging/V failures.
workflow_impact: Corner reduction /, MMMC (multi-mode multi-corner) managementV/SOCV/LVF generation are first-class infrastructure steps with theiroff owners and tooling. Runtime budgeting shifts sign hierarchical and distributed compute.

at_28nm: Static were a back-end signoff step; if it widening and short ECOs fixed it.
at_7nm_5nm: static IR-drop, EM, and thermal are in-loop during placement, CTS, and routing; they directly drive buffer/strap decisions and constraint generation.
why_it_changed: Wire current density and resistance per unit length scale unfavorably; current per unit width of BEOL rises with drive strengths and frequency, so peak currents are close to EM limits. Dynamic IR is a non-trivial fraction of Vdd at activity hotspots.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer defers IR/EM signoff until after route. Symptom: last-mile IR-drop hotspots near clock-tree spines and high-activity regions force global restructure of the clock and P/G, blowing the schedule.
workflow_impact: Power integrity (IR/EM) tools run in parallel with placement and optimization; P/G synthesis and strap pitch are tuned against activity-driven IR maps. Power-aware CTS and vectorless/vector-based dynamic IR become part of the closure flow.

delta_name: Hold closure: localized, easy → global, OCV-dominated
at_28nm: Hold was a local, post-CTS check; fixing meant dropping a small number of delay cells along the path. Skew/derate were modest.
at_7nm_5nm: Hold closure is global and OCV-dominated; every long path needs many delay cells, and skew+OCV derate causes hold fails across the chip on paths previously considered safe.
why_it_changed: Per-cell random and systematic variation scales up; OCV derate applied across long paths can exceed intended hold even with a perfectly balanced tree, especially with multi-cycle paths crossing voltage domains.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer assumes a 'small' hold buffer budget after CTS. Symptom: hold fails across unrelated regions after clock mesh is finalized; fixing-scale buffer addition, area inflation, and reroute.
workflow_impact: Hold fixing is interleaved with CTS and optimization, not a one-shot post-CTS step. Hold-aware CTS, useful-skew tuning, and hold-driven placement/buffering all happen in; signoff runs many hold corners with AOCV/SOCV.

delta_name: Utilization target: 70–80% routine → ~60–65% with hard for closure headroom
at_28nm: Floorplan utilization of 70–80% was routine in many blocks; routing congestion was the dominant constraint and was solved by gentle spreading.
at_7nm_5nm: Effective utilization targets trend lower (mid-60s and below for many high-performance blocks) not because of area but because of pin access, multi-patterning blockage, power strap needs, and clock mesh headroom.
why_it_changed: Per pin count and pin density rise, BEOL pin-access windows shrink-strap density rises, and clock mesh consumes more area; the headroom consumed by closure infrastructure leaves less for random logic.
what_breaks: A 28nm engineer presents a 78% utilization floorplan as 'lean' and pushes density. Symptom: closure stalls on pin-access DRC, IR hotspots, hold fails, and clock-mesh-routing blockage; schedule slips despite area 'savings.'
workflow_impact: Floorplanning includes explicit closure headroom budget (pin-access, P/G, CTS blockage) and target utilization is set per region with margins; utilization is no longer the headline metric of a 'good' floorplan.
